analysis.one_liner: Repeals rules requiring public companies to disclose CEO pay ratios, conflict mineral use, mine safety records, and payments to governments.
analysis.headline: A bill to strip four Dodd-Frank disclosure requirements died in the Senate Banking Committee after a single hearing, never reaching a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase four transparency rules created by the 2010 Dodd-Frank financial reform law. Public companies would no longer have to report the gap between their CEO's pay and their typical worker's pay, whether they use minerals mined with armed groups in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, safety violations at their mines, or the payments they make to foreign governments and the U.S. government for oil, gas, and minerals. It would also bar the Securities and Exchange Commission from writing similar rules again.
analysis.who_benefits: Large public corporations — especially oil, gas, and mining companies and their executives — benefit, because they would no longer have to publish information on executive pay gaps, mine safety violations, conflict mineral sourcing, or payments to governments. The bill also forbids the SEC from issuing substantially similar rules in the future, making the repeal permanent.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil, gas, and mining companies and executives

how_it_helps.text: Removes the requirement that public companies disclose the ratio of their median employee's pay to their CEO's pay, and orders the SEC to repeal the rule it wrote under that provision.

Strikes Section 1502 of Dodd-Frank, which required companies to report their use of conflict minerals from the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Section 1504, which required oil, gas, and mineral companies to report payments to foreign and federal governments.
Strikes Section 1503, which required disclosure of health and safety information at mines operated by the issuer.
Prohibits the SEC from promulgating any rule substantially similar to any of the repealed rules.

analysis.who_pays: If passed, ordinary investors and the public would lose the information these disclosures provide: shareholders could not see how CEO pay compares to typical worker pay, consumers and advocacy groups could not verify conflict mineral sourcing, mine workers would lose a public window into company safety records, and citizens of resource-rich countries could not easily see what companies paid their governments for oil and minerals.
analysis.who_pays_short: Investors, mine workers, and resource-rich countries

drawbacks.text: Repeals the SEC pay-versus-performance disclosure regime without any replacement, leaving investors with less information to judge whether executive pay is tied to company results.
Eliminates the conflict-minerals disclosure aimed at reducing funding for armed groups in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, a key concern of the original Dodd-Frank Section 1502.

The bill's title frames the repealed disclosures as 'non-material,' but critics of such repeals argue that pay ratios, mine safety records, and government payments are material to investors, workers, and anti-corruption efforts; the bill offers no substitute reporting.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit is purely to filing companies: less paperwork and no published information that could draw criticism on executive pay, mine safety, or foreign dealings. The cost falls on investors, mine workers, and anti-corruption efforts, which lose the data. Weighing those sides honestly, the public gets nothing in exchange for losing four established transparency rules, and the ban on 'substantially similar' future rules forecloses even partial replacement.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which held a hearing on it in April 2022 but never voted to advance it, and the 117th Congress ended with no floor vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-ND), joined by one Republican cosponsor, introduced the bill on March 24, 2022, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
On April 5, 2022, the Banking Committee held hearings on the bill, printed as S.Hrg. 117-621.
The committee never reported the bill to the full Senate, no vote was ever scheduled, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Investors, mine workers, and anti-corruption advocates are better off because the bill never became law, since the four Dodd-Frank disclosures remain in effect; the companies that would have shed the reporting requirements gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies that would have dropped the disclosures gained nothing

for.name: Sen. Kevin Cramer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the four Dodd-Frank disclosure provisions and referred it to the Banking Committee.

for.name: Sen. Thom Tillis
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor of the bill; the bill was introduced 'for himself and Mr. Tillis.'

sides.party_line_note: Both of the bill's named supporters are Republicans; the bill attracted only one additional Republican cosponsor and never advanced past a committee hearing in a Democratic-controlled chamber.

industries.note: The bill repeals Section 1504, which required oil, gas, and mineral companies to disclose payments to foreign and federal governments. Losing that disclosure keeps their payments to governments for drilling and mining rights out of public view, where citizens of resource-rich countries and anti-corruption groups have used it to track the flow of money.

The bill strikes Section 1503, ending required disclosure of health and safety information at company-operated mines, and Section 1502, ending required disclosure of conflict minerals from the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Mine workers and communities lose a public record of safety conditions, and consumers lose a way to check mineral sourcing.

industries.industry: Large public companies and their executives
industries.note: The bill repeals the pay-versus-performance and CEO pay ratio disclosure requirements, and bars the SEC from issuing substantially similar rules. Executives and companies avoid publishing pay-gap data and pay-performance comparisons that shareholder and worker groups use to press for change.
The SEC would be ordered to repeal rules it had already written and forbidden from issuing substantially similar ones, a direct rollback of its regulatory authority over corporate disclosure.
